lesson.title: The Inductor: Storing Energy in a Magnetic Field
lesson.summary: Introduces the inductor as a coil that resists changes in current by storing energy in a magnetic field, and derives its defining voltage-current relationship.
lesson.body:
You already know that moving charge ,  current ,  produces a magnetic field around it. An inductor is simply a component built to exploit that fact on purpose: it's usually a coil of wire, and winding the wire into loops concentrates the magnetic field that each turn produces, reinforcing it turn after turn instead of letting it spread out and cancel. On a schematic, you'll see it drawn as a series of loops or curls, a visual reminder that it's fundamentally a coil.

Here's the part that matters for understanding *why* an inductor behaves the way it does. A magnetic field represents stored energy, and that field only exists because current is flowing. If the current through the coil is changing, the magnetic field it creates must also be changing. A changing magnetic field, in turn, induces a voltage across the coil that opposes the change that caused it ,  the coil effectively pushes back against any attempt to speed up or slow down the current through it. This is why inductors are described as storing energy in a magnetic field rather than dissipating it as heat: the energy goes into building the field, and it comes back out of the field when the current decreases, rather than being lost.

This behavior is captured in the inductor's defining equation: V = L(di/dt), where V is the voltage across the inductor, di/dt is how fast the current is changing over time, and L is the inductance, measured in henrys (H). Inductance is just a number that tells you how strongly a particular coil resists changes in current ,  more turns, denser winding, or certain core materials all increase L. Crucially, notice what this equation says: if current isn't changing at all (di/dt = 0), the inductor produces no voltage, no matter how large that steady current is. An inductor only "reacts" when current is in the process of changing.

Try a concrete case. Suppose you have a 10 millihenry inductor, and the current through it is increasing at a rate of 100 amps per second. The voltage that appears across it is V = L(di/dt) = 0.010 H × 100 A/s = 1 volt. That volt isn't coming from a battery inside the inductor ,  it's the induced voltage fighting to keep the current from changing so quickly, a direct consequence of the field having to grow to match the new current.

The energy actually stored in that field at any moment depends on how much current is flowing, following E = ½LI². If that same 10 mH inductor is carrying a steady 2 amps, it's holding ½ × 0.010 H × (2 A)² = 0.02 joules, or 20 millijoules, in its magnetic field. If you then tried to interrupt the current instantly, the inductor would resist violently ,  this is exactly why sudden current interruptions in inductive circuits can produce large voltage spikes, since the coil is fighting to keep the current, and therefore its stored energy, from disappearing all at once. Keep this current-resisting, energy-storing character in mind, because it's what will distinguish the inductor's role from every other passive component you study next.
